Reza (reading): “Pak Reza and Bu Nisa, I need enlightenment. Last week my wife, 'Gina,' and I had our first big fight. The trigger was actually trivial, about year-end vacation plans, but somehow it spread everywhere, down to money issues and each other's family. We yelled at each other, said very hurtful words, even brought up small past mistakes that had nothing to do with it. Honestly, there are words of mine I regret. We finally gave each other the silent treatment for two days. Now we've made up a bit, but I'm very worried, Sir, Ma'am. It feels scary, marriage being like this? Will we keep hurting each other whenever we disagree? How do you 'fight' correctly without damaging our relationship?”
(Brief silence)

Nisa: Fajar… thank you for sharing this experience that must feel very uncomfortable and scary. It's very natural to feel worried. That first 'earthquake' often leaves tremors of fear and doubt. But, the good news, Fajar, is: conflict itself can't and doesn't need to be avoided in marriage. Two heads with different backgrounds, wishes, and viewpoints will surely occasionally clash. What needs to change isn't the conflict, but how you both respond to it.

Reza: Agreed. Consider conflict like a rainstorm. It will surely come sometimes. What matters isn't how to stop the rain, but how we build a solid house with a strong roof and good drainage so the house isn't damaged by the storm. We ourselves too… wow, learning about this took a long process, Ma'am. Not automatically good at healthy fighting!

Nisa: (Nodding) The first and most fundamental, Fajar and Gina, and all couples: Always remember the main purpose of debating or arguing with your partner. The purpose is NOT to WIN, not to prove who's right and who's wrong. The purpose is to UNDERSTAND EACH OTHER'S perspective and FIND A SOLUTION TOGETHER. If the goal is already 'I must win,' what comes out will surely be attack, self-defense, and hurting each other.

Reza: Well, because the main goal is understanding and finding a solution, the way of arguing also needs to be regulated. Try, Fajar and Gina, sitting together when the atmosphere is calm, and agree on some 'Rules of Engagement' for when discussion heats up:

Don't Shout: Try to keep your voice tone controlled. Shouting will only heat up the atmosphere and make the message not get through. No Physical/Harsh Verbal Violence: This is non-negotiable. No physical action, throwing things, let alone using rude words, insults, curses, or name-calling (“You're so selfish!”, “You're just lazy!”). Focus on attacking the problem, not your partner personally. Don't Bring Up the Past (That's Irrelevant): This is a 'weapon' often used when angry, but very damaging. Focus on the issue currently being discussed. Bringing up old mistakes only adds fuel to the fire and makes the solution further away. Agree on a 'Time-Out' Mechanism: If emotions are already too high, feeling like you'll explode, or the discussion is going in circles without result, either party (or both) has the right to ask for a pause. Say it nicely, “I need a moment to calm down, my emotions are running high. Let's continue in 15 minutes / tonight when we're calmer.” But, it's important to truly come back to discussing it later, don't use time-out as a way to run from the problem.

Nisa: Time-out is very important. It gives our rational brain a chance to work again after being hijacked by emotion. But, Fajar, besides the rules during a fight, there's one more very crucial step often forgotten after a big fight, namely the REPAIR PROCESS. Even after you find a solution or agreement, there's often still residual wounds or discomfort from words or actions during the fight earlier.
Reza: True. Giving each other the silent treatment for days isn't a solution, it just piles up 'emotional trash' that could explode again later. The repair process involves the courage to:

Apologize Sincerely: Acknowledge your part of the mistake in that fight (for example, “Sorry, I went overboard raising my voice earlier” or “Sorry, my words earlier hurt your heart”). Be Big-Hearted to Forgive: If your partner sincerely apologizes, try to forgive for the sake of the relationship's good. Remember, forgiving doesn't mean forgetting or justifying, but releasing the burden of grudge. Restate Commitment: Remind each other that you're a team and want to improve the relationship.

Nisa: And don't forget, during the discussion process (before, during, or after time-out), practice active listening ability. Not just waiting for your turn to speak or preparing a rebuttal in your head, but truly trying to understand: What feeling does your partner actually want to convey? What need is behind their anger? Use 'I feel…' sentences to express your feelings, avoid 'You always…' sentences that sound like an attack.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Palace Mirror” Segment)
Nisa: Speaking of big fights… (sighing) Pak Reza and I have also been at our marriage's lowest point, experiencing a conflict so intense, it felt like… it was collapsing everything we'd built.

Reza: True. There was a period when our communication was completely deadlocked. What existed was only anger, mutual blame, suspicion, and words that came out just like that without thinking, leaving deep wounds on both sides. We were both equally stubborn, equally felt right, equally unwilling to give in. It felt like at that time… this marriage was on the edge.

Nisa: Getting through that storm was a very painful process and took a very long time. We had to learn to lower our respective egos. Learn to stop attacking each other and start trying to listen to the pain behind our partner's anger. We had to learn to apologize sincerely for the wounds we caused, and learn to forgive even though it felt very difficult. That repair process wasn't easy, there were times we felt like giving up.

Reza: But, amid that storm, we both finally arrived at one realization: we still loved each other, and we still wanted to fight for this marriage. That commitment is what became our anchor. We learned to communicate again from zero, learned to set new rules of engagement, and we didn't hesitate to seek help from a neutral third party to help us see the problem more clearly.

Nisa: So, Fajar, your bad experience with your first big fight, though scary, can become a turning point. A chance to learn to become a better communicator, a better listener, and a stronger team with Gina, if you both have the commitment to learn from this mistake.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Nation's Frame” Segment)

Nisa: A couple's inability to manage conflict healthily is one of the main roots of domestic violence (DV), whether verbal, emotional, or physical. Fighting always colored by shouting, insults, or threats, that's not normal dynamics, that's a form of violence. And this contributes to the high divorce rate in our country.

Reza: A family filled with unhealthy conflict will also produce the next generation who might imitate the same pattern or carry traumatic wounds. Children growing up in an environment full of destructive fighting will struggle to learn how to build healthy relationships in the future.

Nisa: Therefore, learning healthy conflict resolution skills from the start of marriage isn't just an investment for your own household harmony, but also an investment to break the chain of violence and build a more peaceful and emotionally intelligent society. The ability to disagree without destroying each other is an important foundation for resilient families and a civilized nation.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Steps Together” Segment)
Nisa: Let's summarize this 'science of healthy fighting' again:

Remember the Purpose: Understanding & solution, NOT winning. Make Rules of Engagement: Agree on boundaries (No shouting, insulting, bringing up the past, physical action). Use 'Time-Out': Ask for a pause when emotion peaks, but promise to discuss again. Repair is Mandatory: Sincere apology & big-hearted forgiveness afterward. Listen Actively: Understand the feeling & need behind the words. Use 'I Feel…': Avoid 'You Always…'. Conflict is Normal: How you handle it is what matters.
Reza: For this week's “Palace Love Challenge”:

For All Couples: Try discussing and agreeing on just one rule of engagement for when you disagree or start feeling 'heated.' For example: “From now on, we agree we won't yell at each other” or “We can ask for a 15-minute time-out if the discussion starts to stall.” Write this agreement down and post it somewhere easily visible as a reminder. Individual Reflection: Try to recall your last fight with your partner. What's one thing you did that was less healthy? What's one thing you could do better in the next fight?

Nisa: Discuss the rule of engagement you agreed on or your reflection results in our forum. Let's learn from each other and grow into a couple wiser at managing conflict. Use the hashtag #IstanaDamaiSaatDebat.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the Closing)
Nisa: Fajar, don't be afraid. This first fight is a valuable lesson. Use this as momentum to build a healthier way of communicating with Gina. You're a team, even when disagreeing.
Reza: Thank you for listening to Palace Heart Talk. Hopefully we can all get through conflict storms more wisely and come out of them as a stronger couple.

Nisa: See you in the next episode, we'll discuss a feeling that also often arises after marriage: “Why Aren't You Like Before?” or feeling taken for granted. How to deal with it? Stay with us. Wasalamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh.
Reza: See you! Fight healthily and full of love!
(Solution-giving, calming, but also empowering Season 2 podcast outro music begins, then swells and fades out)
11: Episode 2.4: “Why Have You Changed?” — When Love Feels Taken for Granted
(Sound of the same Season 2 podcast jingle, warm and optimistic, maybe with a slightly more reflective melody at the start, then fade out)
Nisa: Assalamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh… How are you, Palace Heart friends? Hope you're always doing well. Back again with me, Nisa Farha…

Reza: …and me, Reza Satria! Last episode we learned about 'fighting healthily,' right. Hope the knowledge is useful for navigating small storms in marriage. Well, Ma'am, today we want to discuss another feeling that also very often lands in couples' hearts, especially after passing the honeymoon phase full of that flutter.
Nisa: What feeling is that, Sir?

Reza: The feeling of… “Why isn't he/she like before?”. The one who used to reply to messages in a flash, now even being read is a blessing. The one who used to give little surprises, now remembering the anniversary date is already good. The one whose pet name used to be “My Darling My Love My Sweet,” now it's “Hey, can you get me some salt!” Hehe. The point is, the feeling of being considered ordinary or taken for granted.

Nisa: (Smiling thinly) Ah yes… a fairly universal feeling it seems, Sir. After the initial euphoria fades, sometimes routine and comfort make us (or our partner) unconsciously stop doing the small efforts that used to make the relationship feel special. This can raise sadness, disappointment, even doubt about a partner's love.

Reza: True. Even though often it's not because the love is gone, but because the flame was forgotten to be watered! Well, this is the feeling our friend 'Rina,' 30 years old, married 2 years, is experiencing. Let's listen to her heart's unease. Go ahead, Ma'am.
(Sound of Nisa reading the email in a gentle, empathetic tone)

Nisa (reading): “Ibu Nisa and Pak Reza, I'm a loyal listener. I married 'Toni' 2 years ago. The first year felt so beautiful, full of attention, little surprises, sweet words every day. But these past few months feel very different. Toni is now very busy with work, and at home more often plays games or watches TV to relax, he says. Little surprises are gone, compliments or sweet words are rarely heard. I feel like… just being considered already there, no longer his top priority. I'm sad and starting to wonder if his affection has decreased or he's already bored with me. Even though I love him so much and try to be a good wife. What's wrong, Ma'am, Sir? How do I bring back his attention like before?”
(Brief silence)

Reza: Rina… thank you for sharing this feeling that must be uncomfortable. It must sting, right, from feeling like your partner's 'center of the world' to now feeling like just a 'household furniture accessory.' Hehe, sorry Rina, that's just an extreme analogy. But seriously, your feeling is valid and natural to feel.

Nisa: True. It's important to first understand, Rina, that the 'honeymoon' phase full of euphoria and extra attention will indeed naturally transition to a more stable and 'normal' relationship rhythm. That's very natural. We can't expect our partner to bring flowers every day or send love poems three times a day forever, right? Hehe. But… this transition to a stable phase does NOT mean the effort to please your partner, small attention, romance, or appreciation should disappear entirely.

Reza: Well, this is the key! Love is often likened to a plant, Rina. If you want it to stay alive, thrive, and bloom beautifully, it must be tended every day. Watered, fertilized, weeded of pests. Can't just be left to grow wild expecting good results forever. This tending needs CONSCIOUS EFFORT from BOTH PARTIES, every day, even if just a little.

Nisa: So, how to 'water' this wilting love plant again? First step, as usual in marriage: COMMUNICATION. But, as we often remind, how you communicate matters. Avoid accusing or blaming sentences like, “Why aren't you ever romantic anymore?!” or “You don't love me anymore, do you?!” That will only make Toni defensive or feel attacked.

Reza: Try using a gentler approach, use 'I feel…' or 'I miss…' sentences. Choose a relaxed time, maybe when you're together before sleep. Say something like, “Honey (or Mas Toni), I sometimes miss when we first got married and used to chat about random things before sleep,” or “I was so happy when you suddenly brought my favorite martabak before, it felt really special.” Convey your longing for a certain form of attention or connection, not as a demand. This opens the door to discussion, not starts a fight.

Nisa: While conveying your longing, it's also important for Rina to try to see and appreciate whatever small form of attention or effort Toni might still be doing now, which we sometimes miss because too focused on what's 'lost.' Is he still working hard for the family? Is he a good listener when you vent about your work? Does he make sure your car is safe to drive? Sometimes, the form of expressing love changes over time and with increasing responsibility. Try seeing it from that angle too. But, of course, Rina's need to feel special, valued, and romantically desired remains valid and needs to be conveyed in a good way.

Reza: Besides talking, also try taking initiative, Rina. Don't just wait for Toni to change. Maybe you can start first? Create a romantic moment your own version. Prepare a special dinner at home with candles (doesn't have to be expensive!). Give him a light massage when he comes home from work looking tired. Leave a little note with encouraging words in his work bag. Sometimes, a small action from us can 'trigger' or remind our partner to do something similar. The term is, lead by example.

Nisa: And don't forget the power of verbal and physical appreciation. Say “thank you” sincerely for the small things he does. Give a warm hug that's a little longer when he leaves or comes home from work. Simple physical touch like this can be very effective for rebuilding a sense of closeness and being desired.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Palace Mirror” Segment)

Nisa: Tending the 'love plant' amid this busyness… wow, this is a challenge we face every day, Sir. With an extraordinarily packed presidential schedule, endless meetings, work visits, not to mention personal and extended family matters… it's very easy for us to get trapped in 'functional' mode. Just discussing schedules, state issues, household logistics.

Reza: True. Sometimes we only realize, “Huh, this week we haven't really chatted casually, have we?” or “When was the last time we held hands while watching the news?” Hehe. Because of that, we learn to be very intentional in creating and maintaining connection moments.

Nisa: We have a few small 'rituals' we try to maintain. For example, however busy, we try to have breakfast together for a few minutes without talking about work. Or, we have a special 'code' if one of us feels we need more attention. We also learn not to hesitate to say, “I miss you” or “Thank you for being here.” Small things, but with a big effect for keeping the flame alight.

Reza: And we also realize, we can't read each other's minds. If I feel I need something from Madam (for example, need to be listened to without a solution), I have to convey it. Likewise the other way around. So, Rina, don't assume Toni knows what you feel or want. Tell him in a good way. Conscious effort and two-way communication is the key.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Nation's Frame” Segment)

Nisa: This feeling of being 'considered ordinary' or taken for granted in marriage, if left to drag on, can become a time bomb. This is one common cause of dissatisfaction in marriage, loneliness despite being paired, and can lead to cracks or even divorce. Families whose members feel unvalued or unloved are vulnerable to internal conflict.

Reza: Besides that, when emotional and affection needs aren't met within the household, this can open a gap for one or both partners to seek validation or attention outside. Risk of infidelity can increase if the core connection in marriage has become very loose.

Nisa: Therefore, growing a culture of mutual respect, actively appreciating, and making conscious effort to maintain connection in marriage is important not only for a couple's happiness, but also for the stability of the family as society's smallest unit. A strong marriage, where both partners feel loved and valued, will create a more positive environment for children's growth and development and contribute to the nation's social resilience overall. Tending daily love is part of tending the nation's future.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Steps Together” Segment)
Nisa: So, for Rina and Palace Heart friends who feel their love is starting to be taken for granted:

Normalize & Validate: It's natural for the rhythm to change, but your feeling needs to be heard. Communicate Your Longing: Convey what you miss using 'I feel/miss…', not accusing. Appreciate What's Still There: Try to also see other forms of attention from your partner. Take Initiative: Don't just wait, create your own version of a moment. Set an example. Return Appreciation: Say thank you, give a warm touch. Daily Conscious Effort: Remember, love is a plant that needs tending by both, every day.
Reza: For this week's “Palace Love Challenge”:

Option 1: Do one small unusual (but sincere!) action to show appreciation or affection to your partner this week. Could be a little note, a specific compliment, their favorite dish, or just an extra hug. Option 2: Try starting a conversation with your partner using the sentence “I miss when we used to…” (fill in with the activity or moment you miss). See how the conversation develops.

Nisa: What was your partner's reaction to your effort? How did you feel afterward? Share it in our discussion forum or use the hashtag #IstanaRawatCintaHarian. Let's encourage each other to keep tending our love plant!
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the Closing)
Nisa: Hopefully those little sparks can light up again, Rina. Never stop trying to tend your relationship with small, love-filled ways.
Reza: Thank you for being with us on Palace Heart Talk. Remember, a little effort every day can make a big difference in maintaining household warmth.

Nisa: See you in the next episode, we'll discuss another dilemma that often arises: My Career vs. Your Career! What if partners' ambitions clash or demand sacrifice? Wow, exciting, especially for modern couples! Stay with us. Wasalamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh.
Reza: See you! Don't forget to water your love plant today!

12: Episode 2.5: My Career vs. Your Career — When Ambitions Collide
(Sound of the same Season 2 podcast jingle, warm and optimistic, maybe with a more dynamic, modern music touch, then fade out)
Nisa: Assalamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh… Welcome back to Season 2 of Palace Heart Talk! I'm Nisa Farha…

Reza: …and I'm Reza Satria! Wow, time flies, Ma'am, we've thoroughly unpacked the twists and turns of early marriage in this Season 2. From the shock of facing reality, in-law drama, learning to fight healthily, to keeping the flame of love burning.

Nisa: True, Sir. Hopefully our chat can equip friends who are just starting or going through this early marriage phase. Well, to close Season 2, we'll discuss one more challenge very relevant in this modern era, where more and more husband-wife couples both have strong career ambitions.

Reza: Namely… when one partner's career ambition appears to 'collide' with their partner's career, or with family plans already made together. The moment when a golden opportunity comes, but demands big sacrifice from the other party. How to navigate it as a team?

Nisa: This is a complex dilemma, because it concerns personal dreams, commitment to a partner, and also the family's future vision. And this fits perfectly with a heart outpouring from our friend, 'Adi,' 32 years old. This outpouring also feels very personal to me. Let's listen together.
(Sound of Nisa reading the email in a serious but empathetic tone)

Nisa (reading): “Ibu Nisa and Pak Reza, I've always admired your partnership in carrying out your respective roles. I need advice. My wife, 'Karina,' just got an extraordinary job promotion offer at her company. This has been her dream for a long time and I'm very proud of her. The problem is, this promotion requires us to move to another island, or at least Karina will very often travel for work assignments out of town for a long period, maybe years. On one hand I'm very happy for her, but on the other, I'm extraordinarily anxious. What about my own career that's also on the rise in this city? What about our plan to start trying for a baby next year that we've already discussed? I feel so selfish thinking about my worry while my wife is achieving her dream, but this anxiety and confusion is real. How should we best face this dilemma as a team, without anyone feeling sacrificed or regretful later?”
(Brief silence)

Reza: Adi… thank you very much for sharing this dilemma that must feel very heavy. First, congratulations to Karina on her promotion! Amazing! And second, Adi, your feeling — proud yet anxious, happy for your wife but also worried about yourself and shared plans — is NOT SELFISH AT ALL. It's very human and very natural. Don't judge yourself for feeling that. In fact, your awareness of this complexity and your desire to find a solution as a team shows your maturity.

Nisa: Exactly right. The first and most important step, Adi & Karina, is reframing the problem. Don't see this as “Karina's Career vs Adi's Career” or “Karina's Career vs Baby Plan.” But see this as “A NEW Opportunity & Challenge for TEAM Adi-Karina.” How can your team navigate this golden opportunity while also handling the logistics, career, and family plan challenges that come with it? This needs very open, very honest, and very deep communication. Not just talking about the technicalities of moving or work travel schedule, but talking about each other's feelings, worries, fears, and hopes.

Reza: Try, you two set aside truly calm, undisturbed special time. First step: Celebrate Karina's success first! Acknowledge how much this means to her, appreciate her hard work. Make her feel fully supported in this happy moment. After that, then move into discussing the impact. Try making a list together:

What are the pros and cons of this opportunity for Karina's career & happiness? What are the pros and cons (including risks & worries) of this opportunity for Adi's career & happiness? What are the pros and cons of this opportunity for your plans as a family (baby plan, finances, lifestyle)? Write everything down honestly, don't hide anything for fear of hurting. Adi, convey your worries with the intent of finding a solution together, not to obstruct or make Karina feel guilty.

Nisa: Then, after all the cards are on the table, try looking at the big picture. What's your long-term vision as a couple and family? Is Karina's career opportunity, though challenging, actually aligned with that big vision? Is there a way to align it? Does the 'sacrifice' that might be needed (from either Adi or Karina) feel like a shared investment for a better future, or actually feel like a one-sided heavy burden that could cause regret? This needs deep reflection. Pak Reza and I, for example, every time we face a big decision that impacts one party (and usually impacts Pak Reza more because of my role), we always try to return to our shared vision for this nation, and see that decision as a team step, even though not always easy.
Reza: After seeing the big picture, time to brainstorm creative solutions as a team! Don't fixate on just 'yes' or 'no' choices.

Could Adi find an equivalent or even better job opportunity at the new location? Needs research. Could Karina negotiate some aspects of her new job (e.g., travel frequency, possibility of partial remote work)? Could the baby plan be agreed together to be postponed temporarily with mutually understood consequences? If having to LDR (Long Distance Relationship) temporarily, what's the strategy for maintaining intimacy and communication? Is there a need to add support system at home (e.g., household assistant) to ease the burden? Open all possibilities, think outside the box.

Nisa: Adi, your support for Karina's career and dreams is very important for your wife's happiness and your marriage's harmony, especially in today's era. But that support isn't the same as sacrificing all your own ambition silently. There must be discussion, negotiation, and compromise that feels fair to both parties. Maybe there's a phase where Adi supports more, but maybe in the next phase it's Karina's turn to support Adi? This is about take and give in the long run. Whatever decision you make later — moving together, LDR, or even declining that promotion (if that's indeed best for your team) — make sure it's a JOINT DECISION that has considered all aspects maturely and feels closest to a win-win solution for both of you.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Palace Mirror” Segment)

Nisa: Speaking of career dilemma and sacrifice in marriage… I think there's no more extreme example than what we've been through, right, Sir. When I decided to run in the political contest until becoming President, that was a decision whose impact was extraordinarily huge, not only for me, but especially for Pak Reza and our family.

Reza: True. In terms of my personal career in the creative and business world, of course there were so many adjustments, even big sacrifices that had to be made. The role of 'first gentleman' is a role I never imagined, with all its protocol and limitations. But, like Madam said earlier, that was a decision we made together as a team, based on a bigger vision we both believed in.

Nisa: And I'm very aware of the 'price' Pak Reza had to pay. Because of that, I try my utmost to keep supporting his interests and world outside the Palace, despite all the time and space limitations. Our communication about this never stops. How does Sir feel? What need of Sir's isn't met? How can I support Sir better?

Reza: And conversely, my support for Madam isn't just passive support. I try to actively understand the challenges of her job, become a discussion partner, become the calm 'home' she returns to. We continuously negotiate about time, roles, and expectations. Not always easy, often exhausting, but commitment to this partnership is what makes us persist. So, Adi, career dilemma in marriage is real, but can be faced if there's strong will from both parties to work as a team and support each other genuinely.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Nation's Frame” Segment)

Nisa: A husband-and-wife couple's ability to navigate dual career dilemmas like this is very important for the nation's progress. We're in an era where women's contribution in the workforce and economy is increasingly significant. If marriage actually becomes an obstacle for women (or men) to reach their best career potential because of lack of partner support or unresolved role conflict, this is a loss for that family itself and also for the nation.

Reza: Poorly managed career conflict can also become a source of chronic stress in the household, trigger dissatisfaction, and potentially add to divorce rates. We need adaptive modern families, where husband and wife can support each other to grow professionally and personally.

Nisa: Encouraging gender equality in the household, including in terms of career support, is part of building a more just and productive society. Couples who can compromise and work together facing this career challenge are a real example of true partnership that becomes the foundation for resilient families and, in turn, a strong nation.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Steps Together” Segment)
Nisa: So, for Adi, Karina, and all couples facing career dilemmas:

Validate Your Feelings: Proud yet anxious is natural, not selfish. Frame as a Team: This is 'OUR' opportunity & challenge, not 'you vs me'. Deep Communication: Open all cards (hopes, fears, pros-cons) honestly. See the Shared Vision: Does this align with your long-term goals? Brainstorm Creative Solutions: Don't fixate on black-and-white choices. Support ≠ Total Sacrifice: There must be take and give & fair compromise. Make the Decision Together: Ensure the final decision is a team agreement.
Reza: For this Season 2 closing “Palace Love Challenge”:

For Couples (especially dual-career): Try taking time this week to ask and listen to each other: “What's your career dream or target in the next 1-3 years? And how can I support you better to achieve it?” If facing a specific dilemma (like Adi): Try using the pros & cons list method (For Me, For You, For Us) as a discussion guide with your partner to be more structured.

Nisa: What was the result of your discussion? Was there a new understanding that emerged? Share your insight in our discussion forum or use the hashtag #IstanaKarirBersama. Let's learn together to build a strong partnership!
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the Season 2 Closing)
Nisa: With this episode ending, there's still one more, Sir, the closing episode.
Reza: What's that, Ma'am?

Nisa: SE·CRET!! HAHAHAHAH!! Make sure you join us again for the Season 2 closer of Palace Heart Talk. See you! Keep guarding love, guarding communication, and keep working as a team. Wassalamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh.
Reza: Ah, Madam, you're something else!! Well then, see you in the final episode of Season 2!! Success always for all your love and careers!

13: Episode 2.6: Expectation vs. Reality (Again!) — The Trap of 'Perfect' Standards
(Sound of the same Season 2 podcast jingle, warm and optimistic, maybe with a slightly more cheerful but also reflective intro music, then fade out)

Nisa: Assalamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh… Welcome back to Palace Heart Talk, friends. A little surprise, we're briefly back to Season 2: The Gateway to Marriage and Early Reality. I'm Nisa Farha…

Reza: …and I'm Reza Satria! True, Ma'am. After our discussion yesterday, it feels like there's one important aspect of the 'Expectation vs Reality' theme in early marriage we need to dig into again, before we continue to the next life chapter. If in episode 2.1 we discussed the shock of facing practical reality (housework, habits, money), today we want to discuss expectation whose source is more from within.

Nisa: Exactly right. Namely internal standards we often set for ourselves as a husband or wife. Standards about how we should behave, what we must be able to do, how an 'ideal' household should look. And these standards… often unconsciously formed not from discussion with our partner, but from what we see outside — on social media, in movies, or even from comparing ourselves with friends or other family.

Reza: Well, these overly high or unrealistic internal standards are what often becomes a 'trap,' Ma'am. Makes us always feel lacking, always failing, even though our partner might actually be fine and not demanding much. In the end we wear ourselves out, stress ourselves out, and can't enjoy a marriage that might actually already be good enough.

Nisa: Exactly like what many of our listeners might feel, and reflected in 'Siska's' (31 years old) situation we briefly discussed in the previous Season. Let's bring up her situation again as an illustration. Siska felt like a failed wife and often extraordinarily tired because she felt she couldn't meet the 'dream wife' standard she saw in others: the house always spotlessly tidy, cooking always delicious and varied, while still having to succeed in her career, and maybe also always look perfect. Even though her husband himself might never demand all that. But Siska set that standard for herself and felt burdened by it.
(Brief silence)

Reza: Siska, and all Palace Heart friends who might feel similarly… virtual hug first! The feeling of being pressured by a 'perfect' standard is very real, especially nowadays where social media seems to continuously display other people's lives that (seemingly) have no flaws. It feels like we're demanded to be a superwoman or superman who must do everything perfectly, right?
Nisa: True. And the first step to get out of this trap is realizing and challenging the ideal standard that burdens us. Try, Siska (and friends), ask yourself honestly:

Whose standard is this actually? Is this really your own standard, or a standard you adopted from Instagram, from your mother, from your friend? Is this standard REALISTIC for your current condition (with all your busyness, energy limitation, and resources you have)? Does pursuing this standard really make you HAPPY, or actually makes you STRESSED, TIRED, and FEELING NEVER ENOUGH? Answer this question honestly.

Reza: And always remember, friends: What we see on social media is often just the 'front stage' or highlight reel. We never know what happens in the 'kitchen' or behind the scenes. Your friend whose house is always tidy, maybe she has a helper who comes every day. Your neighbor who always cooks a complete menu, maybe she sacrifices her sleep time or hobby. A couple that looks affectionate in every photo, maybe behind the scenes they also often have big fights. Never compare your 'messy kitchen' with someone else's 'shiny display window.' That's unfair to yourself!

Nisa: Focus on managing expectations toward YOURSELF. Give yourself permission not to be perfect. It's totally fine for the house to be messy sometimes because you're exhausted. It's totally fine to order food from outside when you don't have time to cook. It's totally fine to feel overwhelmed and need rest. You're an ordinary human, not a super robot. Try changing the target from 'perfect' to 'good enough.' Celebrate your small achievements in carrying out your role, however small. And most importantly: Prioritize your mental and physical health above the demands of that unrealistic ideal standard. I too, with such high public expectation on my role, had to learn hard about this. Learning to stay grounded in the reality of my capacity as an ordinary human and practicing self-compassion, being kind to myself, when making mistakes or not meeting expectations.

Reza: Besides managing expectations toward yourself, it's also important to align our expectations toward our PARTNER and RELATIONSHIP. Is your hope for your husband (or wife) realistic? Do you expect him to read your mind about what you want? Do you compare him with someone else's husband/wife? Remember, he's also an ordinary human with strengths and weaknesses. Don't burden him with an ideal standard that might only exist in your head. Communicate your needs and expectations clearly and openly, don't assume he 'should already know.' And learn to accept and appreciate your partner as they are right now, not continuously focusing on their shortcomings or on the 'ideal' figure you imagine.

Nisa: Try also discussing TOGETHER with your partner: What's the definition of a 'happy household' according to BOTH OF YOU? Not the Instagram version, not your parents' version, not the neighbor's version. Maybe your version is a house that doesn't always have to be super tidy, but full of laughter and warmth? Maybe a simple dinner but full of deep conversation? Maybe you're both totally fine with ordering food occasionally? Find your own internal happiness standard as a team. Siska, try inviting your husband to talk about this feeling of yours. Ask him, what's his actual expectation of you as a wife? Maybe he doesn't have as high an expectation as you imagine and actually appreciates your presence as you are and happy?
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Palace Mirror” Segment)

Nisa: This internal and external expectation… wow, this is an 'enemy' I have to face every day, Sir. Public expectation on a female President, expectation as a wife, as (formerly) a mother. It feels like the list never ends. If I tried to meet all those expectations, I would have collapsed long ago.

Reza: True. I saw myself how Madam had to learn hard to filter 'voices' from outside, and listen more to her own heart's voice and priorities truly important to her. Learning to dare appear as she is, with all her strengths and (yes, human) weaknesses.

Nisa: The key for me is returning to the core values I hold, to the big goal I want to achieve, and to self-acceptance. I realize I can't please everyone. I realize I can't be perfect in all roles. I learn to focus on what I can control, do my best according to my capacity, and forgive myself when I make mistakes or don't meet a certain standard. And this man's unconditional support and acceptance, seeing me as Nisa as I am, greatly helps me get through the pressure of those expectations.

Reza: I too learn not to be burdened by people's expectation of how a 'first gentleman' should behave. I try to be myself, support Madam in my own way, and focus on what's truly important for our relationship, not on the image in the public's eye. We define the 'success' of our partnership based on our own internal standard.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Nation's Frame” Segment)

Nisa: The culture of comparing ourselves and the pressure to appear perfect, increasingly worsened by social media, has a significant negative impact on society's mental health, especially the younger generation and women. This can trigger anxiety, depression, eating disorders, burnout, and chronic feelings of worthlessness.

Reza: Besides that, unrealistic expectation on marriage and husband/wife roles also contributes to household dissatisfaction. When reality doesn't match the imagined 'fairy tale,' many young couples feel disappointed and give up more easily, which could be one factor in the high early divorce rate.

Nisa: Therefore, growing a realistic attitude, self-compassion (being kind to oneself), media literacy (so as not to be easily swayed by perfect images), and the ability to define happiness based on internal values is important for individual mental resilience and family harmony in Indonesia. We need to together fight the 'must be perfect' narrative and celebrate more the uniqueness and learning process of each individual and couple.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Steps Together” Segment)
Nisa: Let's summarize again how to manage this expectation trap:

Realize & Challenge the Ideal Standard: Whose standard is it? Is it realistic? Does it make you happy or stressed? Lower Your Self-Expectation: Change the target from 'perfect' to 'good enough.' Prioritize Your Sanity: Mental & physical health matter more than a perfect image. Communicate with Your Partner: Convey your feelings & ask about their actual expectation. Appreciate Reality: Focus on the good in yourself, your partner, & your relationship now. Define Happiness Your Version: Make an internal standard together with your partner.

Reza: For this Season 2 closing “Palace Love Challenge”: Personal Reflection: Try identifying one expectation or 'perfect' standard you often burden yourself with (as a partner, parent, worker, etc.). This week, try consciously lowering that standard a bit and practice speaking better to yourself if you don't achieve it. Partner Discussion: Try inviting your partner to chat casually this week. Ask: “In your opinion, what's your most important expectation of me as your partner?” You might be surprised by an answer that could be much simpler than you imagined.

Nisa: How did it feel trying to be kinder to yourself or hearing your partner's real expectation? Share your learning in our discussion forum. Let's support each other to break free from the perfection trap! Use the hashtag #IstanaRealitaBahagia.

14: Episode 3.1: More Than Roommates — Reigniting a Dimming Flame
(Sound of a new podcast jingle for Season 3, maybe with a calmer, more mature, slightly reflective melody, but still warm, fade out)
Nisa: Assalamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh… Welcome back to Palace Heart Talk, friends. It feels great we can continue this journey into the Third Chapter. I'm Nisa Farha…

Reza: …and I'm Reza Satria! In Season 2 we sailed through the excitement of early marriage, right, Ma'am. From shock adaptation to learning to navigate conflict and career. Well, now we level up! We enter a phase where marriage has run quite long, maybe over a decade or two.

Nisa: True, Sir. A phase where the big early waves might have been successfully passed, children might be growing up, career more established. But… it's precisely amid this 'calm' that new challenges no less complicated often appear. One of them is when a couple feels their relationship has become… hmm, too placid?

Reza: Placid but flat, right, Ma'am? Hehe. When husband and wife feel more like good friends sharing a roof and bills, or an efficient household management team, but the spark of love and passion as romantic partners starts dimming, maybe even extinguished. Feeling more like a roommate than a soulmate.

Nisa: The term is roommate syndrome. This is a very common phenomenon in long-term marriage, friends. Busyness, work stress, focus on children, monotonous routine, all of it can unconsciously erode emotional and physical intimacy slowly, until we only realize it when it already feels flat. And we'll discuss this thoroughly today, based on a heart outpouring from our friend, 'Indah,' 45 years old, married 20 years. Go ahead, Sir.
(Sound of Reza reading the email in a gentle, understanding tone)

Reza (reading): “Ibu Nisa, Pak Reza, my marriage with my husband, 'Budi,' has run 20 years. Our children are already teenagers. Generally, our household is fine, no big conflict, financially stable. But that's exactly the problem, Ma'am, Sir. It feels like we're just good friends sharing a house. Our daily conversation is only about the kids' schedule, Budi's work, or the electricity bill. Physical touch is very rare, just holding hands or hugging almost never happens. Intimate relations maybe only once a month or even less, and honestly it feels more like an 'obligation' or routine, no more passion or deep connection like before. Sometimes we avoid it because it feels awkward. I feel something important is missing between us, but I'm confused how to talk about it or start it again without sounding strange or demanding after such a long 'placid' period. Is this normal at our marriage's age? Can it be fixed?”
(Brief silence)

Nisa: Indah… thank you for sharing this honesty that must not be easy. Your feeling — feeling like roommates, missing closeness, but also feeling awkward or confused how to start again — believe me, is experienced by so many couples who've been together a long time. This doesn't mean your marriage failed or your love is gone. Often this is the result of a slow 'erosion' caused by life's routine and busyness. So, yes, this is normal to happen, but that doesn't mean it should just be accepted as is.

Reza: The good news, Indah, is this can definitely be fixed! As long as… well this is the key, as long as both parties (you and Budi) both realize something is 'missing' and both want to commit to trying to reignite it. This can't be from just one side. Like a campfire starting to die out, it needs more firewood added and to be fanned again by both of you so it can burn warmly again.

Nisa: And this effort must be deliberate, Indah. Can't just rely on leftover time or energy after a full day of work and managing the house. Intimacy, both emotional and physical, needs to be prioritized and scheduled, just as important as a meeting schedule at the office or a school pickup schedule. Might sound unromantic, scheduling intimacy? But believe me, amid life's busyness, if not scheduled, it will often be forgotten.

Reza: So, where to start? Maybe the first step isn't straight to bedroom matters, because often the physical flame goes out because the emotional flame already dimmed first. Try starting by rebuilding the emotional connection bridge.

Light Nostalgia Chat: Try triggering a relaxed conversation about your beautiful times together before. “Do you remember when we first dated watching movie X? That was fun,” or “I saw an old photo of us on vacation at beach Y yesterday, I miss those times.” This can revive positive feelings buried by routine. Express Longing (Not Complaint): Try saying gently, “Mas, I miss chatting casually together with you like before, not just about kids or work,” or “I feel we've been a bit distant lately, I miss our closeness.”
Nisa: After the emotional bridge starts rebuilding, the next step is to schedule quality time together regularly and CONSISTENTLY. This is non-negotiable!

Might feel strange or forced at first, but just do it. Can start from something simple: dinner out (without the kids!) once a week, an evening walk together in the neighborhood every weekend, or just sitting together on the porch after the kids sleep, chatting about anything over tea. The key: During that quality time, turn off the TV, put away phones, look into your partner's eyes, and truly be present and listen. Focus 100% on your partner.
Reza: Well, once emotional connection and quality time have started rebuilding, then we can slowly approach the 'sensitive area' of physical intimacy.

Start with Non-Sexual Touch: This is important for rebuilding physical comfort and safety. Try holding hands more often while walking or watching TV. Give a longer, tighter hug when saying goodbye in the morning or welcoming them home. Give a gentle back rub or light shoulder massage when they look tired. Remind your bodies again of the language of affection through touch. Only After That, Dare to Talk About Sex: This might be the most awkward but most necessary part. Choose a very private and relaxed time. Communicate carefully, avoid blaming. Focus on your feelings and desires. “Mas, I feel our intimate life lately has been a bit monotonous, I miss the passion like before,” or “Is there something new you'd like to try together?” or “What makes you feel comfortable and aroused?” Also listen to what Budi might feel or need. Maybe he feels the same but doesn't know how to express it?

Nisa: It's also important to appreciate your partner's body as it is now, with all the natural changes that happen with increasing age. Don't compare with how they looked 20 years ago or with outside standards. Focus on connection and shared pleasure now. Maybe a little creativity is needed? Creating a more romantic bedroom atmosphere? Trying different timing? What matters, communicate openly and respectfully.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Palace Mirror” Segment)

Reza: Keeping the marriage flame burning after so long… wow, this is lifelong homework, right, Ma'am? We too, honestly, have to continuously learn and try. Routine, extraordinary work pressure, responsibility as parents, all of it can easily make us forget to be 'lovers' to each other.

Nisa: True. There are times we feel more like very solid work partners in carrying out state and household duties, but forget the romantic aspect. We have to consciously remind each other. Sometimes I remind Sir, “Sir, when was our last date?”, sometimes Sir suddenly gives a small surprise that makes me feel like 'Nisa' again, not just 'Madam President.'

Reza: We learned that scheduling a date isn't something 'embarrassing' or 'unspontaneous,' but actually a form of our commitment to keep this relationship alive amid the storm of busyness. We also learn to keep communicating about our intimate needs, even though sometimes awkward. Needs and preferences can change over time, and if not discussed, assumptions or disappointment can arise.

Nisa: So, Indah, what you feel can definitely be addressed. But it does need strong intention, conscious effort, open communication, and teamwork from you and Budi. Don't give up on tending your love garden again.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Nation's Frame” Segment)

Nisa: A long-term marriage that loses emotional and physical intimacy, or falls into roommate syndrome, often becomes vulnerable. The feeling of emptiness and disconnection can open the door for one or both partners to seek 'pleasure' or emotional connection outside the marriage, which risks causing infidelity and household destruction.

Reza: Besides that, the quality of parents' relationship greatly affects the atmosphere in the home and children's wellbeing, even teenagers. Children can sense the 'coldness' of their parents' relationship, and this can impact their sense of security and how they view marriage later.

Nisa: Therefore, maintaining vitality and intimacy in long-term marriage isn't just a couple's personal matter, but also contributes to family resilience as a pillar of society. Families whose parents stay emotionally and physically connected tend to be more stable, happier, and become a model of healthy relationships for the next generation. Tending the marriage flame is part of tending a better national future.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Steps Together” Segment)
Nisa: Let's summarize the steps to reignite a dimming flame:

Realize & Share Intention: Acknowledge the problem and commit together to change. Prioritize Time Together: Schedule quality time regularly & consistently. Rebuild Emotional Connection: Start with light chat, nostalgia, express longing. Non-Sexual Touch First: Rebuild physical comfort & safety. Discuss Sexual Intimacy: Honestly, openly, without blame. Listen to your partner. Appreciate Your Partner Now: Value your partner's body and effort as they are. Conscious Effort & Teamwork: This needs daily commitment from both.
Reza: For this week's “Palace Love Challenge,” for friends who feel their relationship is starting to become 'too placid':

Option 1 (Emotional Focus): Schedule one quality chat session (at least 30 minutes, no devices!) with your partner this week. Topic is free, but try to make it NOT about household logistics or kids. Could be about feelings, dreams, or beautiful memories. Option 2 (Physical Focus): Consciously do one type of non-sexual touch every day for the coming week that you might rarely do anymore (e.g., holding hands while walking, a longer good morning/night hug, a back rub). Notice its impact on your feelings and your partner's.
Nisa: What's different after trying this challenge? Share your experience in our discussion forum or use the hashtag #IstanaNyalakanApiLagi.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the Closing)
Nisa: Indah, Budi, and all couples struggling to keep the embers alive, remember, it's never too late to go back to tending your love and intimacy. A little effort every day can bring big change.
Reza: Thank you for starting Season 3 with us on Palace Heart Talk. Keep guarding the connection of heart and body with your partner, whatever your marriage's age!

Nisa: See you in the next episode, we'll discuss another phenomenon that often haunts middle age: Mid-Life Crisis! What if your partner suddenly becomes restless, questions their life, and starts acting strange? How to deal with it? Interesting! Stay with us. Wasalamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh.
Reza: See you! Don't let the flame go out!
(Calm, mature, reflective, but hope-giving Season 3 podcast outro music begins, then swells and fades out)
15: Episode 3.2: Mid-Life Crisis? — When a Partner Suddenly Becomes Restless and Changes
(Sound of the same Season 3 podcast jingle, calm, mature, and reflective, maybe with a bit of contemplation-evoking music, then fade out)
Reza: Welcome back to Palace Heart Talk, friends. Our safe space to talk about the heart. I'm Reza Satria…

Nisa: …and I'm Nisa Farha. Last episode we discussed how to reignite a possibly dimming flame of romance in long-term marriage. The key is in conscious effort and communication. Well, today we'll discuss another phenomenon that also often appears at a more mature marriage or individual age, around 40s or 50s. A phenomenon often called by the somewhat dramatic term: Mid-Life Crisis.

Reza: Mid-Life Crisis! Wow, just hearing it makes your heart race, right, Ma'am? Hehe. The moment when a partner who's usually calm, established, focused on work and family, suddenly becomes restless, questions their life, or even acts 'strange' — buying a big motorcycle even though they never liked motorcycles, starting to dress differently, hanging out with younger people, or becoming more indifferent to home.

Nisa: True, Sir. Although the term 'crisis' might not always be accurate — sometimes this is more a transition phase or deep reflection — but its impact on a partner and family can be very confusing, painful, and scary. It feels like someone we've known for years suddenly turned into someone else.

Reza: And we panic, “What's going on? Is he bored with me? Is he unhappy with this life? Could there be… someone else?” Those questions naturally arise. Well, this confusion and fear is what our friend 'Anita,' 48 years old, is experiencing regarding her husband, 'Bram,' who just turned 50. Let's listen to her story.
(Sound of Reza reading the email in a serious, empathetic tone)

Reza (reading): “Ibu Nisa, Pak Reza, I ask for your enlightenment. My husband, 'Bram,' just turned 50 a few months ago. Since then his behavior has changed quite drastically. He used to be calm and very focused on work and family, now often looks distracted, complaining that his life feels 'the same old thing' and boring. Suddenly last month he bought an expensive big motorcycle without much discussion with me, saying it's 'to get his spirit back.' He's also started coming home late often because of hanging out or joining a motorcycle club with office friends much younger than him. His attention to me and the kids (who are already in college) feels reduced, more indifferent. When I ask, he just says 'I want to find a new atmosphere and spirit.' I'm confused, sad, and honestly, scared, Ma'am, Sir. Scared he'll do something crazy, scared something will happen to our marriage. What's actually happening to him? And what should I do?”
(Brief silence)

Nisa: Anita… thank you very much for sharing your heart's unease that must feel very heavy. I can very much understand your confusion, sadness, and worry. Seeing a partner who's been a family pillar for decades suddenly appear 'shaky,' questioning their life direction, or doing impulsive things, can really shake our sense of security.

Reza: But, before we panic or assume the worst, it's important to first try to understand, Anita, what usually happens in this mid-life phase? This phase (usually around age 40-60) often indeed becomes a moment of big reflection for many people, both men and women. A moment when we look back (what have we achieved?), look forward (what else do we want to achieve? What to do with the rest of our life?), and often wonder about life's meaning (purpose).

Nisa: Questions like “Is this all my life is?”, “What's my contribution?”, “Am I happy?”, “Have my old dreams been achieved?” often arise strongly. Sometimes triggered by a certain event (child leaving home, parent's death, health problem, or simply a 'round' age number like 50), sometimes also appearing just like that. So, Bram's behavior change might not be solely because he's bored with you or the family, but more because of an internal struggle he's experiencing in seeking new meaning or spirit at this life phase.

Reza: However… well this is important, even though the internal struggle is natural, how he expresses it must not go to the point of harming himself or hurting those closest to him. Buying a big motorcycle without discussion, ignoring the family, that's clearly not a healthy way. This is where Anita's role as a partner becomes very crucial, even though it must be very difficult.

Nisa: So, what can Anita do? First step, try approaching Bram with EMPATHY and NON-CONFRONTATIONAL COMMUNICATION first. Avoid directly criticizing his motorcycle or new habits. Try focusing on his feelings. Choose a calm time, approach him gently, maybe while holding his hand, and ask: “Mas, I've noticed you've been distracted lately, seems like you have a lot on your mind? Is there something bothering your thoughts or that you want to talk about?” or “I heard you say you want to find 'new spirit.' What kind of spirit do you actually feel is missing or that you want right now, Mas?” Try digging first into what's behind that behavior, without judging.

Reza: While trying to understand him, it's also important for Anita to convey HOW his behavior IMPACTS you and the family. Again, not accusing or nagging, but use 'I feel…' sentences. For example, “I feel a little worried and lonely when you often come home late without clear news,” or “I'm sad because our time together as a family has really decreased lately.” He needs to know that his actions have consequences on the people he loves. And it's also important to maintain healthy BOUNDARIES in the household. For example, reaffirming the agreement that big purchases must be discussed together.

Nisa: Also try reminding him of the beautiful journey you've been through together. The sweet memories, the heavy challenges you've successfully conquered as a team. Sometimes, amid the restlessness of seeking 'something new' outside, people forget how valuable the 'treasure' they already have at home is. Maybe Anita could offer, “What if we try finding that 'new spirit' together, Mas? Maybe we could try a new hobby together that we've never done before? Or plan a vacation to our dream destination?” Redirect his searching energy toward something more positive and involving the family.

Reza: However, if communication feels stuck, Bram becomes increasingly closed off or defensive, and his behavior becomes increasingly worrying or even destructive (for example, starting to lie, uncontrolled overspending, indication toward infidelity), then don't hesitate to suggest PROFESSIONAL HELP. Could be individual counseling for Bram so he can explore his feelings with expert guidance, or couples counseling for you both to be able to communicate better.

Nisa: Suggesting counseling might not be easy, could be rejected at first. But convey it with good intention, “Mas, I love you and our marriage. I see you're not doing well, and I feel that way too. Maybe we need outside help to get through this difficult phase together?” Remember, seeking professional help isn't a sign of weakness, but actually a sign of strength and commitment to improve the situation. We both believe in this too.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Palace Mirror” Segment)

Nisa: This mid-life phase… (smiling thinly) I feel we're both also entering or starting to enter it, right, Sir. Of course, with the role and responsibility we carry, maybe the form of reflection is a little different. For me personally, amid the extraordinary pressure and routine as President, questions about 'meaning,' 'legacy,' 'is all this worth it?' definitely occasionally cross my mind.
Reza: Me too. There are moments when I reflect again on my identity outside my role as Madam President's companion. What else can I contribute? What personal dreams do I still want to pursue?

Nisa: But what maybe differs is how we try to channel that reflection or restlessness. We learn to talk about it with each other, even though not always easy. We try to find a positive and constructive outlet. I might channel it by writing or initiating a new program I believe is beneficial. Pak Reza returns to his music or creative projects.

Reza: We don't choose the shortcut of doing impulsive things that could hurt ourselves or our relationship. We learn that this reflection phase can actually become an opportunity to grow into a wiser and more authentic person, if faced with awareness and good communication. And a partner's support in this process is very valuable.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Nation's Frame” Segment)

Nisa: This mid-life crisis or mid-life transition issue is very closely related to society's mental health. If not managed well, restlessness at this phase can develop into depression, anxiety, or addictive behavior. The stigma of seeking professional help related to mental health issues at a mature age is also still quite high in our society.

Reza: And the social impact can be significant. Destructive behavior due to unmanaged mid-life crisis often ends in divorce, family financial ruin, damaged parent-child relationships, even decreased work productivity. This is a loss of experienced human resources who should be able to keep contributing positively.

Nisa: Therefore, increasing awareness and understanding about this mid-life phase, normalizing discussion about mental health at all ages, and encouraging individuals and couples to seek support (both from partner and professional) when facing difficulty, is part of the effort to build a more resilient and stable society. Families who can get through the mid-life transition healthily will become a more solid pillar for the nation.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Steps Together” Segment)
Nisa: So, for Anita and everyone accompanying a partner who's 'restless' at middle age:

Understand & Empathize First: This might be their internal struggle, not about you. Approach Without Confrontation: Ask about their feelings, not criticize their behavior. Communicate Impact & Boundaries: Convey your feelings & maintain family rules of the game (e.g., about finances). Remind Them of Your Shared Journey: Invite them to find positive 'new spirit' as a team. Don't Hesitate to Suggest Expert Help: If communication is stuck or behavior is destructive. Take Care of Yourself: Don't get sucked into their restlessness too. Your mental health matters too.
Reza: For this week's “Palace Love Challenge”:

For those who feel their partner (or themselves) is in this phase: Try starting a conversation focused on feelings and hopes for the next life phase, not on problems or complaints. Ask, “What are you most grateful for right now?” or “What's one thing you want to do or achieve at our age now?” For all listeners: Try taking 15 minutes this week to reflect on your own feelings about aging and your life's meaning now. What excites you? What might you need to adjust?
Nisa: This reflection is important for all of us. Share your thoughts (if you're willing) in our discussion forum or use the hashtag #IstanaNavigasiParuhBaya.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the Closing)

Nisa: Anita, hopefully this conversation can give you a little guidance. This phase is indeed not easy, but with patience, the right communication, and healthy boundaries, hopefully Bram can get through it without destroying the valuable things you've built together.
Reza: Thank you for listening to Palace Heart Talk. Hopefully we can all navigate every life phase more wisely and with full support.

Nisa: See you in the next episode, we'll discuss another source of conflict that also often gives parents headaches: Different Parenting Styles! How to unite vision when father is permissive, mother is strict, or vice versa? Wow, this will surely be exciting! Stay with us. Wasalamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh.
Reza: See you! Stay calm facing the mid-life storm!
(Calm, mature, understanding and hope-giving Season 3 podcast outro music begins, then swells and fades out)
16: Episode 3.3: Different Parenting Styles — When Father Says 'Yes,' Mother Says 'No'

Nisa: Assalamualaikum warahmatullahi wabarakatuh… Welcome back to Palace Heart Talk. The place we share stories, learn together, and grow together. I'm Nisa Farha…

Reza: …and I'm Reza Satria! Last episode we talked about the mid-life 'storm,' right, Ma'am. How to accompany a partner who's restless searching for meaning. (Sound of Nisa reading the email in a sympathetic, understanding tone)

Nisa (reading): “Ibu Nisa and Pak Reza, my husband, 'Rendra,' and I very often argue about how to raise our children who are 8 and 6 years old. For example about discipline, I tend to be stricter. If they break a rule, I apply clear consequences, like reducing playtime or no TV. Meanwhile my husband, Rendra, is more permissive and easily feels 'sorry for them.' He often secretly cancels my 'punishment' or defends the children in front of me. Same with screen time, I want to limit it to a maximum of 1 hour a day, Rendra often just lets it be as long as the kids are calm and don't disturb his work. As a result, the kids get confused about which rule actually applies, and now they're very smart, whenever I'm angry or applying a rule, they immediately run to 'take shelter' with their father. This makes me very frustrated, feeling alone in parenting, and feeling my authority as a mother is weakened. We end up bickering over this almost every day. What's the solution, Ma'am, Sir?”
(Brief silence)

Reza: Yanti… oh, Bu. It must feel really exhausting being in that position. Already tired managing the kids, plus having to 'fight' with your own partner about how to raise them. The feeling of frustration, feeling alone, and feeling weakened is very understandable to us. And the dynamic of smart kids 'finding loopholes' to the more lenient parent is indeed classic but real.

Nisa: True. But before we talk solutions, the first important step is trying to first understand the root of the parenting style difference between Yanti and Rendra. Often, this difference isn't because one doesn't care or deliberately wants to break the rules, but because of their own upbringing background as children, values they believe in, or even their different innate temperament. Maybe Rendra was raised very harshly so he doesn't want his child to feel the same? Or maybe Yanti was raised with high discipline and feels that's the best way? Try to first understand the reason behind your partner's parenting style, not immediately judge 'you're too soft!' or 'you're too harsh!'. Your intentions are surely the same: wanting the best for the children.

Reza: Well, after there's an effort to understand each other (even if not immediately agreeing), the next step that's absolutely necessary is: SIT TOGETHER SPECIALLY — without the children present! — to MAKE A JOINT AGREEMENT about basic principles and rules of engagement in parenting. Doesn't have to be exactly 100% the same in every small thing, but for important issues that often become a source of conflict like:

Rules about discipline and consequences (What's allowed/not allowed? What's the consequence for breaking them? Who enforces it?) Rules about screen/gadget time (How long? When? What content?) Rules about bedtime, mealtime, type of food. The main values you want to instill (Honesty? Responsibility? Empathy? Independence?). Discuss this thoroughly, find a compromise or middle ground you both can agree on and carry out together.

Nisa: Why is this agreement and unity so important? Because children are excellent observers and clever negotiators! Hehe. If they know their Father and Mother aren't of one voice, they'll cleverly exploit that gap. They'll run to whichever party is more 'advantageous' to them at that moment, like what Yanti experienced. This not only makes the rules ineffective, but also confuses the child about what's right and wrong, damages their respect for parental authority, and in the long run isn't good for their character formation. Parental consistency and unity is the main key in effective parenting.

Reza: After the agreement is made together, the commitment to carry it out TOGETHER is the most challenging but mandatory part. This means: Supporting Each Other in Front of the Child: If Mother is applying an agreed consequence, Father must support it (even if inside he feels sorry), don't weaken it or defend the child in front of Mother. Likewise the other way. Show that you're one team. Discuss Disagreement Privately: Even if there's disagreement about how to handle a specific situation, or feeling your partner is too strict/lenient at that moment, never argue or criticize each other in front of the children! Hold it in, discuss it later when you're alone together. In front of the children, always show a united front.

Nisa: If discussing together feels stuck or you need a new perspective, don't hesitate to seek additional reference together. Maybe try reading the same popular parenting book? Attend a parenting seminar or workshop together? Or even consult a child psychologist if needed? Sometimes getting input from a neutral third party can help open a new perspective and find a more effective solution. And don't forget, appreciate your partner's effort in raising the children, even though their style differs. Focus on their good intention.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Palace Mirror” Segment)

Reza: Raising Alex (Nisa-Reza's son in the novel) before… wow, there were definitely small differences of opinion between me and Madam. I might tend to be more… relaxed? Prefer inviting play and exploration. While Madam, with her very structured background…

Nisa: (Smiling) Maybe I emphasized more about time discipline, academic responsibility, or the importance of reading books, right, Sir? Hehe. Nisa: We'd discuss each other's reasons. Why am I worried? Why does Sir feel it's important? Then we'd find a middle ground. For example, okay he can try that new thing, but with extra supervision or safety gear. Okay he can play games, but the time is limited and we choose the content together. That agreement is what we then conveyed and carried out together consistently.

Reza: And we saw its impact on Alex. When he knew his Father and Mother were of one voice, he felt safer, the rules were clearer, and he respected those rules more. He couldn't 'run' to either party to seek justification. Our unity as parents gave him a stable foundation.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Nation's Frame” Segment)

Nisa: Parenting inconsistency and open conflict between parents in front of children can have a very significant impact on child development, friends. A child can grow into someone confused about boundaries, anxious, manipulative, or even lacking respect for rules and authority figures. This can carry through into adulthood.

Reza: Besides that, a household continuously colored by parents' bickering about the children also isn't a conducive environment for healthy child mental development. This can become one factor contributing to children's behavioral problems at school or in society, and even perpetuate unhealthy parenting patterns to the next generation.

Nisa: Therefore, parents' ability to work together as a solid and consistent team in raising children is a crucial investment for the nation's future. We're not just shaping one child's character, but helping shape the next generation's character. Families who can align their parenting vision will produce children who are more emotionally stable, more responsible, and more ready to become good citizens.
(Soft Music Transition — Entering the “Steps Together” Segment)
Nisa: Let's summarize the keys to a solid 'Parent Team':

Understand the Root of the Difference First: Recognize your partner's parenting style background, avoid judging. Agree on Basic Principles & Rules: Discuss together (without the kids!), find compromise for important issues. Apply Consistently & Together: Support each other's rule enforcement in front of the child. Don't Argue in Front of the Child: Discuss disagreement privately. Show a United Front: Show that Father & Mother speak with one voice. Seek Reference/Help If Needed: Books, seminars, or professionals. Appreciate Your Partner's Effort: Focus on their good intention.
Reza: For this week's “Palace Love Challenge,” especially for parents:
